item.title: Protected Logical Qudits in Kitaev Quantum Double Models via Stable Representations
item.description:
Pay dirt new method — Introduces ε-stable representations ρ⊗ε≃ρ for 1D irreducible representations ε of order d, proving they yield protected d-dimensional logical qudit subspaces with cyclic shift XL implemented by ribbon operators. Realizes logical qubits in Sn (n≥3), a logical qutrit with universal gates in A4, and qudits for any d≥2 via (ℤ2)d⋊ℤd.

Grade 0.474 · 3.4σ above the day's baseline · matched “Surface codes: Towards practical large-scale quantum computation” · Naihong Hu, Futao Wang

Asks

What general group-theoretic conditions allow finite-group Kitaev quantum double models to support protected logical qudits?

But

Universal computation construction assumes existence of deterministic quasiparticle transport operators Mξρ.

Tools

Kitaev quantum double models D(G) · Finite-group representation theory · Ribbon operators · ZX-calculus

Abstract

Fault-tolerant quantum computation requires robust protection of encoded quantum information. In this work, we develop a representation-theoretic framework for constructing protected logical qudits in finite-group Kitaev quantum double models. By introducing ε-stable irreducible representations, we establish a necessary and sufficient existence criterion and derive ribbon--projector commutation relations that yield a d-dimensional protected logical subspace. We apply this construction to symmetric and alternating groups, obtaining logical qubits for S_n (n≥3) and a logical qutrit for A₄. Moreover, the family (Z₂)^drtimesZ_d realizes protected logical qudits of arbitrary dimension d≥2. Finally, for D(A₄), we describe a scheme for universal logical qutrit computation using ribbon-based logical operations.

item.title: Fast Fault-Tolerant Decoders for Hypergraph Product and Lifted-Product Codes
item.description:
Pay dirt new method — Derives message-passing decoders from parent classical LDPC decoders to resolve stabilizer-induced trapping sets directly, decoding lifted-product codes on a phenomenological graph without auxiliary CNOT variable nodes or OSD post-processing.

Grade 0.470 · 3.4σ above the day's baseline · matched “quantum LDPC codes and low-overhead fault tolerance” · Asit Kumar Pradhan, Nithin Raveendran, David Declercq, Bane Vasić

Figure

Classification of product nodes in the base graph of HGP and LP codes, showing VV-type and CC-type variable nodes alongside X-check and Z-check nodes.

Asks

How can QLDPC decoders achieve fast, fault-tolerant decoding under circuit-level noise without OSD post-processing and auxiliary CNOT correlation nodes?

Before

BP+OSD (BP_OSD) required cubic-complexity linear-system solves over large Tanner graphs expanded with auxiliary correlation nodes for CNOT faults.

But

Evaluated on lifted-product (LP) codes under circuit-level noise through simulations.

Tools

hypergraph product (HGP) codes · lifted-product (LP) codes · message-passing decoders · stabilizer-induced trapping set analysis · phenomenological Tanner graph modeling

Abstract

We design low-complexity, fault-tolerant decoders for quantum low-density parity-check (QLDPC) codes with the goal of reducing decoding latency. We target two major bottlenecks of decoding under the emphcircuit-level noise model: (i) post-processing via order-statistics decoding (OSD), and (ii) the large number of auxiliary variable nodes commonly introduced to represent CNOT-induced correlations during syndrome extraction. Our key observation is that propagating CNOT faults (emphhook errors) create emphstabilizer-induced trapping sets (TSs) that are intrinsic to hypergraph-product (HGP) and lifted-product (LP) constructions. Therefore, instead of modeling each such fault with an explicit correlation node and relying on OSD to clean up the resulting failures, we design message-passing decoders that resolve the corresponding emphstabilizer-induced TSs directly. We obtain these decoders by deriving QLDPC decoders from decoders for the parent classical LDPC codes and using them collectively to correct broad families of emphstabilizer-induced TSs. For CNOT faults that manifest primarily as syndrome errors, we show that their effect is equivalent to a data error together with syndrome-bit measurement errors. Consequently, given repeated measurements and a decoding graph that already includes nodes representing syndrome-bit errors, no distinct variable node is needed for each CNOT fault. Using a emphphenomenological Tanner graph with nodes representing only data errors and syndrome-bit errors, simulations on the LP codes show a reduction in, or comparable, logical error rates relative to BP+OSD, at substantially lower decoding complexity.

item.title: Neutral atom quantum computing
item.description:
Pay dirt review — Surveys the physics, current status, and scaling bottlenecks of neutral atom quantum processors across alkali (87Rb, 133Cs) and alkaline-earth-like (88Sr, Yb) architectures.

Grade 0.433 · 2.8σ above the day's baseline · matched “Suppressing quantum errors by scaling a surface code logical qubit” · M. Saffman

Figure

Images and arrangements of large neutral atom arrays across different atomic species, showing arrays scaling from 1,000 to over 12,000 sites.

Asks

What is the physical and architectural status of neutral atom systems for scalable fault-tolerant quantum computing?

But

Circuits currently limited to a few hundred operations due to recoil heating, atom loss, SLM pixel bounds (<105 sites), and optical power dissipation.

Tools

optical tweezer arrays · Rydberg blockade gates · laser cooling · quantum error correction · shuttling tweezers

Abstract

Neutral atom qubits are one of the leading approaches for implementation of a large scale quantum computer. The original proposals for neutral atom qubits were formulated more than 25 years ago, with first demonstrations of a universal gate set following 10 years later. In the last few years the performance and scale of neutral atom qubit arrays has developed at a rapid pace leading to demonstrations of quantum algorithms, and logical qubits for fault tolerant error correction. This contribution reviews the physics of the neutral atom approach, surveys current capabilities, and provides an outlook for future progress.

item.title: Quantum Block Turbo Codes
item.description:
Pay dirt new method — Formulates quantum block turbo codes using product structures of constituent stabilizer codes. Fifth iteration of [[64,9,9]] QBTC achieves estimated word error rate of 6×10−7 at 10−2 depolarizing rate.

Grade 0.405 · 2.4σ above the day's baseline · matched “Sparse-Graph Codes for Quantum Error Correction” · Khaled Jebari, Luiz Anet Neto, Ramesh Pyndiah, Jean-Louis de Bougrenet de la Tocnaye

Figure

Plots word error rate against channel depolarizing rate. Shows turbo decoding iterations improving error rates for [[8,3,3]]×[[8,3,3]] code compared to single-qubit product code and message-passing baselines.

Asks

How to adapt classical block turbo codes and iterative product-code decoding to quantum error correction.

But

Depolarizing channel simulation. Requires classical soft-information processing for component decoders.

Tools

stabilizer codes · product codes · iterative decoding · SISO decoders · symplectic representation

Abstract

In the early nineties, the introduction of turbo codes revolutionized classical error correction. The idea was mainly applied on two types of codes: convolutional turbo codes and turbo product codes. The first type of codes was adapted to quantum error correction which initiated the theory of quantum serial turbo codes. In this paper, we present a theory for quantum block turbo codes, the quantum analog of the second type of turbo codes. We describe their iterative decoding algorithm and simulate their performances on a depolarizing channel for different constituent codes.

item.title: Bosonic codes from compact phase spaces
item.description:
Pay dirt theory — Bosonic codes on hyperbolic Riemann surfaces (g≥2) have stabilizer groups π1(Σg) that are non-amenable, forcing a strictly positive spectral gap in Hˆstab that precludes normalizable states satisfying all stabilizer conditions.

Grade 0.403 · 2.4σ above the day's baseline · matched “bosonic codes: cat, GKP, and autonomous stabilization” · David Roberts, Aaron Slipper, Alireza Parhizkar, Victor V. Albert, Mohammad Hafezi

Figure

Panel (d) shows the average stabilizer energy ⟨Hˆstab⟩(t) versus protocol rounds t. A single generator (s=1, amenable) drives energy toward zero, while multiple non-commuting generators (s=2,3,4, non-amenable) hit a non-zero 𝒪(1) plateau dictated by the spectral gap.

Asks

What bosonic quantum error-correcting codes emerge when phase space is a compact Riemann surface of genus g≥2?

But

Holds for compact Riemann surfaces with genus g≥2. Non-amenability prevents normalizable code states even approximately.

Tools

Riemann-Roch theorem · automorphic forms / Poincaré theta series · Fuchsian groups · geometric quantization · stellar representation

Abstract

We present the algebraic structure of bosonic quantum error-correcting codes on genus-two Riemann surfaces. We explicitly construct the code words as automorphic forms and analytically generate the full tower of code spaces at all weights. We prove a fundamental no-go theorem: for any genus greater than one, the stabilizer group is non-amenable, forcing a strictly positive spectral gap in the stabilizer Hamiltonian. Consequently, no normalizable quantum state can satisfy all stabilizer conditions. This sharply contrasts with standard Gottesman-Kitaev-Preskill (GKP) codes, where the amenability of the stabilizer group Z² permits approximate code words with arbitrary precision.

item.title: Universal recovery in approximate quantum error correction
item.description:
Pay dirt theory — A single recovery map simultaneously corrects every ℰ-controlled channel with worst-case error bounded by environment-leakage distance and average-case error bounded by Knill--Laflamme Hellinger distance. For fixed code and error set, the average-case optimal error of channel-dependent recovery is achieved by a single universal recovery map.

Grade 0.395 · 2.3σ above the day's baseline · matched “High-threshold and low-overhead fault-tolerant quantum memory” · Dor Elimelech, Victor V. Albert, Alexander Barg

Asks

Whether uniform protection against ℰ-controlled channels in approximate quantum error correction extends to a universal decoding operation independent of the specific noise channel.

Before

Uniform approximate guarantees were proved separately for each channel in arXiv:2607.22995, requiring channel-dependent recovery maps.

But

Finite-dimensional Hilbert spaces; channels must have Kraus expansions in Span(ℰ) with coefficient matrix norm bounded by 1.

Tools

adversarial error-set model · Petz recovery map · Bény--Oreshkov framework · polar decomposition analysis · Knill--Laflamme Hellinger distance

Abstract

Universal recovery -- the existence of a single recovery map that corrects an entire family of error channels -- is a central feature of quantum error correction (QEC). In exact QEC, linearity guarantees that a code correcting a given error set also corrects every channel whose Kraus operators lie in its linear span, and that a single recovery map suffices for all such channels. Approximate quantum error correction (AQEC), which relaxes perfect recovery to recovery with controlled error, has traditionally lacked this structure. In a recent paper (arXiv:2607.22995), we developed a theory of approximate quantum error correction showing that a restricted form of linearity persists in the approximate setting, yielding uniform AQEC guarantees for the family of channels controlled by a given error set. In this work, we complete the picture by establishing the second half of universal recovery in the approximate setting: a single recovery map can simultaneously correct every channel controlled by a given error set. The error-set theory we proposed quantifies approximate correctability through two parameters: the environment-leakage distance, governing worst-case performance, and the Knill--Laflamme Hellinger distance, governing average-case performance. We show here that both quantities also control universal decoding. We further study the Petz map naturally associated with an error set as an explicit universal recovery, and obtain uniform average- and worst-case guarantees across the entire family of channels.

item.title: Data and code for collision-model Dicke-state preparation: depth-fidelity frontiers, circuit costs, and superconducting-processor measurements
item.description:
Pay dirt new result — Presents dataset across 31 Dicke target states DNK (N=5 to 14, depth m=0 to 200 sub-rounds) and hardware benchmarks on the 54-qubit IQM Emerald processor, where measured circuits retain up to 0.758 of noiseless fidelity.

Grade 0.385 · 2.1σ above the day's baseline · matched “Suppressing quantum errors by scaling a surface code logical qubit” · Duc-Kha Vu, Minh Tam Nguyen, cSahin K. Özdemir, Özgür E. Müstecapliouglu, Fatih Ozaydin

Figure

Unconditional state fidelity F across hardware measurement arms on the IQM Emerald superconducting processor compared to the ideal noiseless fidelity Fideal and native two-qubit gate count.

Asks

How do state-preparation fidelity, circuit depth, and hardware gate overhead trade off when generating multipartite Dicke states via collision models?

But

Circuit depth capped at m=200 sub-rounds; noiseless L1 yields lower bounds rather than certified global optima; 544 of 6,231 cost rows are upper bounds; hardware results reflect a single session on 10 arms without physical excitation-number heralding.

Tools

collision model quantum state preparation · IQM Emerald 54-qubit superconducting processor · permutation-orbit tomography · Qiskit

Abstract

Dicke states are multipartite entangled states in which a fixed number of quantum excitations is coherently shared among many qubits. Originally introduced in the context of cooperative emission and superradiance, they are now important resources for quantum sensing, networking, and collective quantum phenomena. Preparing prescribed Dicke states with high fidelity, however, remains challenging, particularly as the system size and excitation number increase. Here we present an open dataset and accompanying code for preparing Dicke states using a collision-based quantum protocol. The dataset covers systems from five to fourteen qubits over a broad range of excitation numbers and records how the best-found noiseless preparation fidelity changes with circuit depth. It also provides circuit-resource estimates and experimental measurements for selected states on the 54-qubit IQM Emerald superconducting processor. The accompanying code reproduces the processed data and validation checks, providing a reusable benchmark for studying the trade-off between state-preparation fidelity, circuit cost, and hardware noise.

item.title: Size-Independent Robustness in Multipartite Bell Self-Testing
item.description:
Worth a look new result — Analytic robust self-testing bound for n-qubit GHZ states certifies extractability Ξ≥snβ+μ (with sn=(2+1)/2n/2 and μ=−(1+2)) under MABK inequality violation β, maintaining constant noise tolerance independent of party number n.

Grade 0.365 · 1.8σ above the day's baseline · matched “High-threshold and low-overhead fault-tolerant quantum memory” · Shen Cao, Xingjian Zhang, Fei Shi, Qi Zhao

Figure

Asks

How does the robust self-testing bound for multipartite GHZ states scale with the number of parties n under Bell inequality violations?

Before

Existing analytic bounds for general n tolerated violation errors that shrank polynomially (McKague et al.) or exponentially (Sarkar et al.) with n, failing to give nontrivial certification beyond n≥10 even at 10−5 relative violation deficiency.

But

Analytic bound is within a constant factor of 2 in slope from the theoretical upper bound; the exact optimal bound is verified numerically via polynomial-size grid search up to n=100.

Tools

MABK Bell inequality · Kaniewski operator-inequality framework · Jordan's lemma · Naimark dilation · simplex grid search and gradient descent

Abstract

Practical robust self-testing of multipartite entanglement has so far been restricted to small-scale systems due to error bounds that degrade severely with system size. In this work, we establish multipartite self-testing with robustness independent of the size of the quantum network. We derive a fully analytic, device-independent self-testing bound for n-qubit Greenberger-Horne-Zeilinger (GHZ) states. The bound scales linearly with the observed violation error and lies universally within a constant factor of two from a theoretical upper bound. Furthermore, the operator-inequality framework reduces the verification of the conjectured optimal bound to a highly efficient numerical check, which we perform up to n=100. Consequently, GHZ entanglement can be certified under a fixed noise level in arbitrarily large systems, enabling scalable device-independent verification.
